Martin: "Saying security and safety is important, it is with every tech epoch, and we wanna have some oversight. That was very, very sensible. The problem was just couching this notion of pacing."

"There's a number of issues with pacing. First off, it's orthogonal to safety and security. You can slowly build a weapon. That's not different than building a weapon."

"It kind of feels like this kind of almost milquetoast capitulation to the pause people. 'You say pause, well, I say pacing.' Which is almost like pause, but it's not like pause."

Martin: "Nuanced second-order words don't work when people are really afraid... I literally think you should have just been like, 'Safety and security is paramount. We're gonna put in these controls.'"

"Dario's first five words or whatever are, 'We need to pace the frontier.' It just puts you in a very different mindset. What he could have said is, 'We need to secure the frontier.'"

"Pace is like the uncanny valley of making the doomer people unhappy and the policy people unhappy. The doomer people are like, 'That's not a pause, this is pacing.' And everybody else is like, 'This isn't real, you're not gonna do it anyways, and you're not as focused on security.'"

Consumer stocks have been left in the dust.

#Uranium ⚛️ September 19, 2026

$GLO’s latest Dasa update is a warning for the entire uranium sector: tomorrow’s mines will need tomorrow’s prices.

Estimated direct project costs have climbed 74%, from US$375.6M to US$653M versus the 2024 feasibility study. Equipment and infrastructure are up 60%; construction is up 352%.

Some of that reflects Niger-specific delays and costs shifted forward from later operations. But the underlying pressures travel across borders: equipment, labour, construction and the expense of keeping a project alive before revenue begins.

That’s why I expect more uranium developers worldwide to face painful budget revisions as older studies meet actual construction bids.

Higher upfront costs mean more capital to raise, more investment to recover and less room for error. Lenders need confidence in debt repayment. Shareholders need returns that justify the risk.

A brief spot-price spike won’t solve that. Developers need long-term contracts at prices that make new mines financeable.

Without those prices, projects get deferred. Deferred projects mean fewer new pounds, and greater pressure on buyers when they need replacement supply.

My view: substantially higher uranium contract prices will be necessary to unlock enough new production.

The uranium price needed to keep an existing mine running can be far below the price needed to build the next one.

I sat down with Kyle Chassé for a wide-ranging conversation, and he asked the kind of questions that let me get into the ideas I care about.

A few of the things covered:

Bitcoin as life management, not just portfolio management

A family needs runway. A corporate treasurer needs to make payroll no matter what happens to the banking system. Six months of runway in Bitcoin is a hedge against chaos, and I watched that lesson play out when Silicon Valley Bank went down.

Stablecoins as a bridge

They get people comfortable with digital payments and on-chain life. A positive step, even though a coin tied to the dollar inherits the dollar's problems.

The frictionless business

Imagine raising a fund in Bitcoin, entrepreneurs paying employees, suppliers, and taxes in Bitcoin, everything on-chain in smart contracts. Money that moves faster makes society wealthier. Gold and shells slowed the economy down. Bitcoin speeds it up.

AI and your job

You do not have to quit to innovate. Improve your job with AI, get better at it, and let the leadership around you encourage it. The saddle makers became car mechanics. The mathematicians figured out the computer.

Stablecoins as a bridge

AI and your job
